discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: An upper-level ridge will position over the region this evening before waning over the weekend. Areas of fog will be the main concern until the next disturbance arrives Saturday evening with light lowland rain and mountain snow showers. An active pattern will lead into next week as a series of frontal systems bring widespread precipitation, breezy winds, and the potential for minor coastal flooding.
hydrology: Wetter systems moving into the region next week will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely cross into flood stage mid to late week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An upper-level ridge will position over the region this evening before waning over the weekend. Areas of fog will be the main concern until the next disturbance arrives Saturday evening with light lowland rain and mountain snow showers. An active pattern will lead into next week as a series of frontal systems bring widespread precipitation, breezy winds, and the potential for minor coastal flooding.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Sunday night)
paragraphs: The latest forecast remains on track this evening with no updates. An upper- level ridge axis will cross overhead tonight as conditions remain "dry" and stable. Quotations were needed for the word dry in the previous sentence as dewpoint depressions will have little to no spread. REFS model soundings are showing a stout inversion developing tonight across much of W WA. This feature in concert with surface high surface pressure and weak gradients will lead to develop of fog with freezing fog a possibility for portions of southern Puget Sound, southwest interior, and Kitsap Peninsula to name a few. Overnight lows will range between the upper 20s to upper 30s.

A foggy start to the day on Saturday but the pattern will begin to change. An upper-low will position offshore on Saturday, forming a Rex Block as it interacts with a high center in northern BC. This set up will allow for a sub 990-995 mb surface low to meander offshore the WA coast throughout much of the weekend. PoPs are favored to increase on Saturday afternoon as light lowland rain showers and mountain snow showers (snow levels around 2,500 to 3,000 ft) return to the forecast. Showers will continue into Sunday as well but the bulk of the precipitation will remain offshore before transitioning to steadier precipitation overnight along the coast and Olympic Peninsula. Precipitation amounts are not expected to be impactful. Seasonal temperatures are expected in the short-term with highs in the upper 40s to near 50 F and overnight lows in the 30s.
High astronomical tides over the weekend may bring the potential for some minor coastal flooding along the Pacific Coast and the Strait of Juan de Fuca by Sunday.

sections.title: Long term (Monday through Friday)
paragraphs: The aforementioned upper-low will finally get ingested into the mean flow on Monday as a broad upper-trough encompasses much of the NE PAC. Models are picking up on the potential for a well- organized frontal system deepening offshore Monday night into Tuesday. This will open up the pattern to a parade of disturbances, maintaining an active pattern into the latter half of next week. Here we could see widespread precipitation, breezy winds and possible minor coastal flooding as surface low pressure interacts with high astronomical tide along with the potential for high surf.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Northerly flow aloft will become south to southwesterly by Saturday morning as a broad upper level low moves into the Washington offshore waters. The low level flow will become increasingly offshore into Saturday. Overall confidence in the ceiling forecast is somewhat low overnight into Saturday morning as a stratocumulus deck in place across portions of Western Washington has slowed low cloud reformation. Additionally, high level cloud arriving ahead of a trough offshore will act to lessen low cloud coverage. Patchy LIFR fog is still expected overnight in the more fog prone areas of the Southwest Interior and Kitsap Peninsula, but may need to be scaled back elsewhere. VFR ceilings are expected for Saturday afternoon after patchy fog dissipates with any MVFR ceilings likely restricted to coastal areas where showers are most likely.

KSEA...Latest guidance is scaling back fog and low cloud probabilities. Anything that forms will largely be a function of any brief clearing that occurs. Latest REFS has IFR ceiling chances around 30% overnight, but satellite trends shows some of the stratocu deck breaking up. Any low ceilings that form should be gone by 18Z Saturday with gradually lowering VFR ceilings for the remainder of the day. Surface winds light E/SE backing to a more northeasterly direction at 7 knots or less Saturday afternoon.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Benign conditions with relatively light winds and seas around 5-6 ft will continue through this evening. Another round of patchy fog across the Puget Sound and interior Salish Sea will be possible again Saturday morning.

Over the coastal waters, winds will begin to increase overnight as a frontal system begins to approach the Pacific Northwest. Winds will increase Saturday morning, peaking around mid-day. East to southeast winds will reach Small Craft Advisory criteria cross most of the coastal waters and the west and central portions of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Occasional gale gusts are possible across the coastal waters, but confidence is highest in the strongest winds in the outermost waters north of James Island, where the watch was upgraded to a Gale Warning. Winds will stay below headline criteria for most of the inland waters, except over the East Strait of Juan de Fuca starting Saturday evening, where a Small Craft Advisory has been issued through early Sunday morning.

By Sunday, the low center well offshore deepens, which will increase the pressure gradients as it slowly creeps closer to the coast. Winds increase again across the coastal waters on Sunday and remain elevated through Sunday night.

A much stronger low pressure system is on track to arrive Monday into Tuesday with high confidence in strong southeasterly winds across the coastal waters and Strait of Juan de Fuca, with >80% chances for gales through Tuesday evening, as well as a 50-80% chance for storm force gusts across the outer coastal waters from late Monday through much of Tuesday. Winds will begin to ease from their peak Tuesday night into Wednesday but headlines will likely need to remain through the end of the week as low pressure systems continue to move through the area, keeping winds elevated.

Seas will rise early Saturday to around 8-13 ft, primarily from the southerly winds, before the longer period westerly swell arrives Saturday night into early Sunday, pushing seas back up to around 11- 14 ft. Seas will remain around 8-13 ft through Monday when the strong low will bring seas up to 15-20 ft by Tuesday. Ensemble guidance remains confident (60-80% chc) in seas above 20 ft, at least across the outermost coastal waters. Seas will likely remain above 12-15 ft through the end of the week as conditions remain active.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: Wetter systems moving into the region next week will start to bring some rises to area rivers. At this time, no widespread river flooding is expected, however the Skokomish River will likely cross into flood stage mid to late week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Dry weather continues into Saturday morning before an active weather pattern returns. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds starting midday Saturday and continuing through next week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Dry weather continues into Saturday morning before an active weather pattern returns. A series of Pacific frontal systems will bring multiple rounds of rain, mountain snow, and breezy winds starting midday Saturday and continuing through next week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Thursday...Visible satellite imagery early Friday afternoon depicts widespread stratus that had formed overnight slowly dissipating from southeast to northwest across NW OR and SW WA as weak, transient high pressure forms over the region. Stratus may not dissipate completely from far NW OR and SW WA before the sun sets, so these locations may end up with high temperatures a few degrees lower than forecast. Otherwise, high temperatures this afternoon one again are forecast to peak in the mid 40s across the Willamette Valley, 50s along the coast, and 30s along the Cascades. As the high pressure moves inland overnight, there's the potential for another round of fog/stratus forming tomorrow morning, though high clouds moving in ahead of the next weather system could limit that formation.

Today is the last dry day in the forecast through at least Thanksgiving Day. Multiple weather systems are slated to move through the PacNW through next week, bringing the return of a wet pattern. Precipitation returns Saturday as an upper level trough deepens in the eastern Pacific and pushes a frontal system inland tomorrow night into Sunday. Rain is forecast to begin along the coast by late Saturday morning, pushing inland as scattered showers over the afternoon, continuing into Sunday. Latest guidance indicates that the low will spin offshore through the day Sunday before moving northeast and weakening offshore of WA/BC on Monday. Because of this pattern of the low staying offshore, precipitation chances and amounts have decreased inland from yesterday's guidance, with higher precipitation chances of 70-95% over the Coast Range, Willapa Hills, and Coast. This has impacted the Cascade snow forecast, as well. Although snow levels will be around 2500-3500 ft, QPF amounts over these elevations will mainly be less than 0.1-0.25 inch. Therefore, the probability of snow amounts of at least 2 inches is now only 20-40% at pass level for Saturday through Sunday and less than 5% for 4 inches. For elevations higher than pass level, there's a 40-70% chance of at least 2 inches and 15-40% chance for at least 4 inches. Those who have outdoor plans over the high Cascades should still plan on snow covered roads at times, especially in stronger showers.

Ensemble guidance is in good agreement that another low pressure system will deepen in the eastern Pacific early next week, hot on the heels of the weekend system. Ensembles suggest this system will also spin offshore through much of the week, likely pushing multiple frontal systems inland through the week. The next frontal system bringing widespread rain and a period of breezy winds to the region will be late Monday into Wednesday. This system will have more Pacific moisture associated with it than the weekend system with latest ensembles indicating IVT values peaking around 500-750 kg/(ms). From late Monday through 4 AM PT on Thursday, there's a 60-80% chance of at least 1 inch of rain along the coast, 40-70% over the Cascades, and 25-60% for the inland valley, with highest probabilities around and north of the Columbia River. Looking at probabilities for at least 2 inches, those drop to 35-50% along the coast, 10-45% over the Cascades, and 5-20% for the inland valley. No significant flooding impacts are expected at this time, though periods of heavier rain could cause localized ponding of water in lower lying areas. Breezy winds are possible along the coast with the frontal passage on Tuesday, as well. There's a 40-65% chance of peak wind gusts at least 45 mph and a 5-20% chance for peak gusts at least 55 mph.

Beyond Wednesday, ensemble guidance becomes more uncertain on specific details of the low pressure system, though precipitation chances continue through at least Thanksgiving day. There is the indication that another frontal system may push into the region sometime Thursday into late week, causing another round of widespread rain and breezy winds. NBM has a 15-30% chance of peak wind gusts of 55 mph or higher on both Thursday and Friday with a 30-60% chance of at least 1 inch of rain across all of NW OR and SW WA for the 48 hour period ending at 4 AM PT Saturday. Keep an eye on the forecast, especially if you have travel plans for the upcoming holiday. -03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00Z Saturday...Satellite imagery and terminal observations as of early Friday afternoon depicts MVFR stratus across the central and northern Willamette Valley while conditions have cleared out along the coast and southern Valley (KEUG). Given the low sun angle at this time of year, expect this stratus deck will continue through tonight. Ceilings with this stratus deck will most likely lower to high-end LIFR to low-end IFR thresholds by 09-11Z Friday. Guidance suggests a 30-50% chance for IFR CIGs across parts of the Valley at any given hour between 09-16z Sat. The persistent stratus deck should help limit fog development at the surface, however some areas of fog cannot be ruled out, especially at KEUG where skies have cleared out.

Variable winds around 5 kt or less continue through tonight. East/southeasterly winds increase after 12-15z Sat along the coast and at KTTD as pressure gradients tighten ahead of the next system. This system will bring rain showers into the area beginning between 15-18Z Saturday, and should also help lift ceilings to MVFR/VFR thresholds.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Expect the ongoing stratus deck to remain in through tonight with light and variable winds less than 5 kt. MVFR ceilings will most likely lower to the 500-1000 foot range by 10-11Z Saturday. By 18Z Saturday, east-southeast winds will increase with rain showers beginning. This will help ceilings lift to either MVFR or VFR thresholds. -23

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Light southerly winds around 15 kt or less continue across the waters through this evening with seas around 5-6 ft at 11 seconds. The next frontal system arrives late tonight into Saturday, increasing southerly winds with gusts up to 30 kt. Small Craft Advisories are in effect tonight through early Sunday morning. For the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore, isolated gale force wind gusts up to 35 kt are possible. Guidance did not suggest that gales would be frequent or widespread enough to warrant a Gale Warning. High confidence (70-90% chance) for seas building to 8-10 ft on Saturday, and 12-14 ft by Sunday.

Active weather continues next week as a series of systems impacts the waters. There is potential for storm force wind gusts early next week, with a 60-80% chance for at least isolated wind gusts exceeding 48 kt across the outer waters beyond 10 NM offshore. In addition, seas will also build into the mid to upper teens, with a 20-40% chance of exceeding 20 ft on Tuesday for areas beyond 30 NM offshore. For the Columbia River Bar, chances for seas exceeding 20 ft are currently around 5-15%.
Long period swells will also result in a moderate threat for sneaker waves through this weekend. Those visiting the coast should use extra precaution when in or near the water. -10
